column10: 10-day old fry were obtained and kept at 26 °C for 15 days to recover from transportation stress. These fry (n = ?) had a mean length of 15 +/- 1.3 mm and mean mass of 0.385 +/- 0.003 g. Fish were equally distributed into four temperature treatments (1 °C/day change) at a density of 26/75 L. Uniform rearing conditions were maintained in all the experimental groups except for the temperatures (26, 31, 33, and 36°C0. A fixed photoperiod of 12L:12D was maintained with light exposure from 6:00 to 18:00. Aeration was provided in all the experimental containers to maintain the DO level. Other water quality parameters were monitored at every 5-day interval and maintained at the optimum rearing conditions for L. rohita.
column76: Once the fish reached their experimental temperatures, they were left to acclimate for 30 days. Once acclimation was achieved, a feeding trial was carried out for an additional 30 days. Pelleted feeds containing 35% crude protein were used during the feeding trial. Initial feeding was done twice a day (8:00 and 20:00) at 10% of the body weight and gradually decreased based on body weight, which was assessed at each 10-day interval, for up to 30 days. Fish were starved for a day prior to the assessment of standing stock, thermal tolerance tests, and rates of oxygen consumption. % weight gain was calculated with the formula (final wt - initial wt)/ initial wt x 100. FCR was calculated with the formula feed given in dry wt/ weight grain in wet wt. % survival was calculated with the formula (# of fish harvested)/(# of fish stocked) x 100. Thermal tolerance was assessed at the end of the feeding trial (fish were exposed to their experimental temperatures for 60 days total at this point). 12 fish per temperature treatment were randomly selected (e.g., from the 26°C treatment, 6 were randomly selected for CTMax and another 6 for CTMin). These fish were exposed to a constant temperature increase or decrease of 0.3°C/min until LOE, which marked the endpoint of the trial. Oxygen consumption rate was measured for 6 fish from each treatment.

column5: Mean body length was obtained from figure 2 using webplotdigitizer. x-values (lengths) obtained were then averaged in Excel. Due to the nature of this extraction, some points were hidden behind others and therefore could not be identified. Thus, sample sizes of estimated mass do not perfectly match experimental sample sizes. Specifically, 48 masses were obtained in the 15 degree treatment (experimental = 54 n); 35 masses were obtained in the 20 degree treatment (experimental n = 42); 18 masses were obtained in the 28 degree treatment (experimental n = 21). However, 41 masses were obtained from the 25 degree treatment, which exactly corresponds to the experimental sample size.
column10: Sea bass eggs obtained from a broodstock matured and spawned spontaneoussly under controlled photoperiod and temperature conditions. Conditions (temperature, feed, etc.) varied with developmental stage. Juvenile fish were then used for this study. Photoperiod was maintained at 12L : 12D; temperature at 20°C; oxygen saturation at > 90%; and salinity 35 per mille. Fish were fed on commercial crumbs six times per day.
column49: not sure how many/if there were replicates for each temperature treatment, but they specify that the n in table 2 is indeed number of measured individuals
column76: Eighteen hours (0.75 day) prior to taking measurements, fish housed at 20 °C were transferred from the stock population and were starved and acclimated to the test temperatures (15, 20, 25, 28 °C). Then, one fish was placed in the swimming channel for 10 min at 2BL/s water velocity. The water velocity was then increased at a rate of 1 BL/s every 10 min until fish were fatigued and left the swimming channel. Critical swimming speed was calculated according to Brett (1964).

Sample size data: from text, 8-13 fish per tank and 3-6 replicates per temperature treatment.
column10: Wild mahi were caught and brought to the University of Miami Experimental Hatchery. The F1 produced by these fish were the ones used in the study. Thus, the experimental fish were reared from egg to late juvenile/early adult size. They were fed live planktonic prey during early stages, until there occurred a transition to a pelletized diet. The fish used in the study were either at late juvenile or early adult stage. Before the experiment began, fish were transferred and randomly assigned into the experimental tanks at an initial temperature of 22-25°C. See experimental_protocol_notes column for more info.
column49: There were 3-6 tank replicates per temperature and 8-13 fish per tank.
column76: mahi were first placed in tanks set at the temperature of the rearing tanks (~22-25° C) and then were gradually ramped over 48 h to the 4 target temperatures (20, 24, 28, and 32 °C). Fish in different treatments were exposed to the test temperatures for different durations.* Swimming performance was measured for each treatment group. Food was withheld 24-36 h prior to start of swim trials. Mahi were introduced to swim tunnels at a speed of 1 BL/s, and were left to habituate overnight. Swim trials were conducted the following morning. Ucrit was obtained by increasing water velocity from initial 1 BL/s by 0.5 BL/s every 20 min until the fish was fatigued.

column76: Experiments took place from December 1999 to June 2001. Fish were acclimated to their experimental temperature for 12-18 days (and salinity 25-28 per mille). The next morning, metabolic rate trials were conducted. Each experimental run consisted of a 30 min period at each of the designated speeds up to the maximum speed. The speed increment was 10 cm/s, with the speed raised at a rate of 4 (cm/s)/min. The maximum swimming speed (Umax) that fish were able to attain was determined by direct observation.

column76: Fish were acclimated to experimental temperatures (10, 13, 16, or 19°C) for two weeks and were not fed 48 h prior to experimentation. Swimming speed was determined by translating positional data (obtained by automated fish tracking) and calculating the x-y positions from two consecutive immages. column10: Smallmouth buffalo were sampled throughout each calendar season from Jan. 19, 1995 to Feb. 5, 1996. They were collected and transported 97 km to the University of Mississippi in a tank filled with river water. In the lab, they were transferred to dechlorinated tap water. Fish were tested 1-4 d after capture and were not fed in captivity. Stomachs were not examined to confirm a post-aborptive state, but time expired between capture and experimentation for all fish was a minimum of 20 h. An acclimitaization protocol similar to that of Facey and Grossman (1990) were used. That is, fish were held at conditions (seasonal temperature and photoperiod) similar to natural conditions from which they were removed. Thus, spring, summer, fall, and winter buffalo were held and tested under the following temperature and photoperiod regimes, respectively: 20°C & 12L:12D; 27°C & 15L:9D; 17°C & 12L:12:d; 10°C & 10L:14D.

column76: Fish were sampled throughout each calendar season from the Colwater River in Quitman County, Mississippi. Fish were transported to the University of Mississippi and housed in similar conditions to the ones they were acclimated to in the field. Field temperatures (to which the fish were acclimated) were (from spring to winter): 21.3, 27.3, 16.2, and 6.7°C. In the lab, four temperatures and photoperiods were used for each season: 20°C & 12L:12D (spring); 27°C & 15L:9D (summer); 17°C & 12L:12:d (fall); 10°C & 10L:14D (winter). Fish were tested 1-4 days after capture. Specifically (again from spring to winter), the groups of fish were held for: 3.6, 1.4, 3.1, and 2.6 days. Swimming trials were conducted in a swim tunnel respirometer. Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. A variation of the standard critical swimming speed protocol described by Brett (1964) was applied. That is, a 30-minute rest period was allowed between each velocity increment such that the respirometer could be replenished with oxygen. The modified protocol began at a water velocity of 10 cm/s, followed by stepwise increases of 10 cm/s after successful completion of each bout. These increases continued until the fish fatigued. Each buffalo was only tested once. Ucrit was calculated as outlined by Brett (1964): ucrit = U1 + (U2)(t1/t2). VO2s were monitored for 1 hour at each speed increment until the fish fatigued. Active metablolic rates were measured, and standard metabolic rates were estimed by extrapolating the relationship between speed and VO2 to zero activity/zero swim speed.

Swimming trials were conducted in a swim tunnel respirometer. Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. The 9.25Lt fish experienced a range of 6.9-14.9°C, and the 32.70 experienced a range of 3.2-14.6°C. Also -- this paper has a ~similar protocol to Schaefer (1986), where the fish are never acclimated to the test temperature nor really acutely exposed -- but are under a ~daily ramping by 1-2°C. ALSO, for acclim_temp: the fish were acclimated for at least 3 weeks prior to the start of trials to temperatures ranging from 3-6°C. I reported the median value as 3+6/2 = 4.5°C for all three cohorts.
column10: Eggs of Atlantic cod were collected from a group-spawning broodstock in Massachusetts and maintained at NOAA/NMFS in Narragansett, Rhode Island. Eggs were hatched, and larvae and young juveniles were reared in flow-through, 75-L aquaria provided with filtered Narragansett Bay seawater (30 - 32 per mille) in a green-water culture at temperatures between 8-12°C. Larvae were fed rotifers for 3 weeks and were subsequently weaned onto brine shrimp. As juveniles grew, they were provided larger pellet diets.
column76: Three trials were conducted, each using a different group of fish (grouped together based on size). Each group was acclimated (for at least 2 weeks) to a low temperature (3-6°C) and a 14L:10D light regime, and maintained at these conditions within a rearing tank for at least 1 week prior to the start of the trial. Thus, acclim_time_min = 21 days. During each trial, the group of juveniles was videotaped for 3-5 min at the start of every hour during each of the 14 light hours at a specific water temperature. The water temperature was then increased by 1-2°C, and the group was video-taped at the new temperature aftera 26-48h habituation period. The procedure was repeated over the course of 23-28 days. The two-dimensional swimming speed of individual fish was quantified using image analysis. In every trial, 2 of the 14 video-taped time periods (one from first half of day, other from second half) were randomly selected and analyzed. Swimming speed was determined by estimating the change in the position of the snout of individual fish. The mean swimming speed for each time period was based upon the average speed of all individuals.

column10: 133 fish with similar body length (9-13 cm) were selected from the total 347 caught juveniles. The fish were transported to the lab. To reduce stress, the captured wild fish were acclimated for 7 days (20°C, natural photoperiod, DO > 6.5 mg/L) before the start of the experiment. They were fed common commercial fish pellet feed. After this acclimation period, the fish were divided into 4 experimental groups of 32 - 36 fish.
column49: n/a
column76: The fish were divided into 4 experimental groups of 32 - 36 fish. The temperature was ramped by 1°C/day (starting from 20°C) until the experimental temperatures were reached: 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. The fish were allowed to acclimate to their temperatures for 30 days before trials. In each swimming trial, a fish was placed in the experimental arena and left to habituate for 24 h. Fish stress was avoided by controlling the equipment remotely. Before the formal Ucrit experiment, each group’s critical swimming speed (Ue) was predicted. A healthy and uninjured juvenile fish was placed in the swimming area and adapted at a low velocity of less than 0.5BL/s for 2h. The velocity was increased by 0.4BL/s every 2 min until the fish became fatigued and stopped moving. The △U (15% Ue) during the formal experiment was determined accordingly. When formal experiments were started, a juvenile fish was placed at a velocity of 0.5 BL/s for 30 min and then adjusted by 0.5 BL/s every 5 min, and 15% Ue was increased every 30 min after the 60% predicted value until the fish reached a state of exhaustion. The results were recorded, and the critical swimming speed (Ucrit) was calculated. The calculation formula is as follows: Ucrit = Ui - 1 + (T/△T ) x △U, where Ui-1 indicates the sub-high swimming speed of the fish before exhaustion. T indicates maximum swimming speed duration of the fish (less than 30 min), △T indicates 30 min, △U indicates 15% Ue predicted value, Urcrit indicates relative critical swimming speed, and BL indicates the fish body length. Maximum swimming speed was measured using the incremental flow velocity method. A fish was placed in the swimming area and habituated to a flow velocity of 0.5BL/s for 2 h. The flow velocity was gradually adjusted to 1BL/s, then was increased by 0.05 BL ever 15 s until the fish was fatigued and stopped swimming. The flow velocity at this point was considered to be the fish's maximum swimming speed. Tail beat frequency was calculated by replaying video footage and using the formula TBF = TBT/T, where TBT is the tail beat frequency of a fish during the observation and T is the time.

column10: Perch and roach were collected by electrofishing. They were acclimated for 3 weeks in the laboratory before experiments started. There were 12 tanks: 6 with two perch each, and the other 6 with five roach each.
column49: for both species, 6 replicate tanks. for each temperature treatment, the same fish was tested at different prey densities. Though, I don't see how this could be the case for SP12 (perch) as there were only 2 fish per tank, so clearly the same fish had to be tested at multiple temperatures. very unclear. Nonetheless, 6 replicate values for each species, so data represents an average of 6 measurements across tanks for both species.
column76: Fish were acclimatized for 3 weeks in the laboratory before experiments started. There were six aquariums with 5 roach each and six aquariums with 2 perch. Treatment temperatures were 12, 15, 18, and 21°C (+/- 0.1). Prey densities  were 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 prey/L. The pret used was phantom midge (Chaoborus obscuripes). All experiments were carried out with hungry fish to standardize hunger levels. Before an experiment started the fish were confined to a smaller section of the aquarium by a partition. Then the prey was introduced and the experiment was initiated by removing the partitioning and allowing the fish to feed. To avoid satiation effects the experiment was terminated when no more than ten prey had been captured. Data recorded during the experiments were the swimming speed of the fish during feeding, number of attacks and number of successful captures during the experimental time. Only one fish in one aquarium was observed in each experiment rendering six replicates for each species per experiment (number of aquariums = 12). The test fish were re-used at different prey densities within temperatures but were changed between temperatures.

Treatment temperatures were 12, 15, 18, and 21°C (+/- 0.1). Prey densities  were 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 prey/L. The pret used was phantom midge (Chaoborus obscuripes). All experiments were carried out with hungry fish to standardize hunger levels. Before an experiment started the fish were confined to a smaller section of the aquarium by a partition. Then the prey was introduced and the experiment was initiated by removing the partitioning and allowing the fish to feed. To avoid satiation effects the experiment was terminated when no more than ten prey had been captured. Data recorded during the experiments were the swimming speed of the fish during feeding, number of attacks and number of successful captures during the experimental time. Only one fish in one aquarium was observed in each experiment rendering six replicates for each species per experiment (number of aquariums = 12). The test fish were re-used at different prey densities within temperatures but were changed between temperatures.

column76: Fish were caught in their natural breeding grounds in the salt ponds at Atlit ca. 10 . km south of Haifa, Israel in December 1992, using a small seine net. They were brought to the Zoological Garden of Tel Aviv University, where they were transferred to 200-l acclimation tanks, each equipped with a biological filter, aeration and water heater. The salinity of the water was matched to that of the salt ponds. A minimum of 2 months was given for the fish to become acclimated (to the lab? to temperatures?) before starting the experiments.  These wild-caught fish were then allowed to breed and the fry produced were used for the experiments. After some period of growth, only females initial weight: 0.4–0.8 g were used for the temperature experiment, since the territorial behaviour of the males was considered to potentially affect the  results. The experiments lasted for 30 days. Experimental temps were 18, 20, 23, 25 and 27°C.

column10: Paired parent fish were kept in 16 L aquariums @ 24C, with approximately one-third of the water replaced daily to maintain quality. Weekly measurements ensured water parameters were good. The photoperiod was 12 hours light and 12 hours dark, with light intensity at 150 lx. Fish were fed ozone-disinfected frozen blood worm larvae to satiation twice daily.
column49: **mode is based on a number of spawns, but the amount of fish is  6 pairs--also technically 6 replicates (6 pairs in each treatment) but psuedoreplication bc they are all in the same tank
column76: 30 paired parent fish with six replicates were randomly subjected to 18 ℃, 21 ℃, 24 ℃, 27 ℃, and 30 ℃ within a week acclimation at a rate of 1–2 °C/day. The trial lasted for 60 days, maintained from mid October 2014 to mid December 2014 when room temperature was between 14 ℃ and 21 ℃. Water temperature were obtained by heaters and a water cooler (RESUN, CW-1000A, Guangzhou, China) and monitored by sophisticated mercurial thermometer twice daily. After a week of acclimation, spawning was recorded daily at 11:30 p.m. Parents were separated from the eggs and returned to the aquarium the next day. Eggs were transferred to 600 mL containers, and fertilization rates were calculated. Fertilized eggs were incubated at 25°C. Upon hatching, larval counts determined the hatching rate, and deformities were recorded to assess the malformation rate.

column76: Mating and swimming trials were conducted at 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, and 38°C, with individual fish used for only one performance measure (mating or swimming) at one temperature. Experimental fish were exposed to an acute change in temperature at a rate that did not exceed 4°C/h. Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

column76: Mating and swimming trials were conducted at 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, and 38°C, with individual fish used for only one performance measure (mating or swimming) at one temperature. Experimental fish were exposed to an acute change in temperature at a rate that did not exceed 4°C/h. Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

column5: *fish "were collected and maintained as described by van der Lingen (1994)". I consulted this paper to get the info. Citation: Van Der Lingen, C. (1994). Effect of particle size and concentration on the feeding behaviour of adult pilchard Sardinops sagax. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 109, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.3354/meps109001. ALSO, the authors reported results from 19 experiments, and the data presented in the graph (swimming speed vs temp) are inextricable -- impossible to say which point represents which experiment and what the conditions were. While they list 'initial temperatures' used, the temperatures I extracted from the graph do not match those values. I used mine, rounded to the nearest hundredth. n_temps was estimated by counting unique rounded whole# temp values from extraction (which were 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22 = 12 temps). Also, acclimation time was unclear -- when experiments were done at temperatures other than ambient, the fish were habituated for at least 4 days to the test temp. Because of this short amount of time, I put curve type as acute-change. Also, sample sizes were unclear, as well as whether the same fish were used for each experiment (the authors say there were 10 fish, but some weren't considered for swimming speeds, and under figure 2, they wrote n = 117). So, for sample size and cohort_ID --> n/a. There was data on the size of the 10 fish, so size data refers to n = 10.

column10: About 300 flounders were obtained from a hatchery in Japan and transported by air to the Netherlands Institute for Sea Research. The fish were divided among 8 plastic crates and kept at 14°C and a salinity of S=31 for one week. After the week, fish were divided among four tanks in which temperature was gradually adjusted to 10, 15, 20, and 25°C over the course of two weeks. During acclimitization, the fish were fed daily with finely chopped mussel meat and deep-frozen mysids. Mortality was high during the first ten days of acclimatization, when 46% of the fish were lost. For the growth experiment, fish were fed daily with finely chopped mussel meat and mysids. column76: Juvenile common carp were acclimatized to a water temperature of 16°C for 20 days prior to the commencement of experiments. There were 3 fish per tank and a total of 18 tanks. Prior to their introduction into the tanks, the 54 fish were measured (fork length and mass). The experiments involved the recording of the fish feeding reponses to different food densities through filming for a maximum of 5 minutes. Once the trials at 16°C were complete (after 20-day acclimation and 52-day trial period), the second phase of the study began, where the 54 fish were split into three different groups: 20°C, 24°C, and 28°C. Temperature was increased by 0.5°C/24h until target temperatures were reached, and once they were, the fish were allowed to habituate for 5 days before experiments began once more. During each thermal period, the feeding rates and functional response of the carp were quantified by presenting the fish with either maggots and pellets once daily, with the number of food items released (density) chosen randomly from 148, 222, 296, 370, 519, 740, and 111 items per square meter. The food items were released into the tanks across their entire surface area. At the end of each filming, any uneaten food was removed immediately. The feeding reponse treatments were completed approximately every 72 h. When the fish were not subjected to feeding response treatments, routine feeding was maintained at 2% body weight per day, using maggots and pellets alternately. The feeding rate was the mean time taken by a fish to ingest the fifth item and expressed as the number of items taken per second. During data analyses, the use of multiple individual fish in the tanks was accounted for using linear mixed effects models. The influence of food density on feeding rate was tested through determination of the functional response.

Parameters a and b were unknown and were estimated by fitting the equation to the observed functional response data using non-linear least squared regression.

column10: Caught fish were transported to Fairfield University and placed in 340 L tanks where individuals were acclimated to either 20, 15, 10, or 5°C. C-start trials began on the third week of acclimation, so I put acclim_time_min as 21 dyays.. Fish were fed with a combination of squid, worms, and crabs triweekly. Some fish died over the course of the experiments and sample sizes were adjusted accordingly.

column76: On the third week of acclimation (4 temps: 5, 10, 15, 20°C), each individual was placed in a 45 cm x 90 cm tank with a depth of 15 cm. C-starts (i.e., escape responses) were recorded from above at a rate of 250 frames/s. Each fish was startled by dropping a rubber ball directly in front of the snout to ensure that the orientation of the stimulus was similar for all individuals. Four C-start trials were recorded for each fish at each temperature. To avoid fatigue, each fish was allowed a 10-minute rest period between trials. Fast-start analysis followed Gerry, Robbins, and Ellerby (2012). Approximate straight-line center of mass and snout movements were tracked using  ImageJ. The COM and snout position data were used to calculate the heading of the fish. The heading angle of the fish relative to the Y-direction was calculated as angle = tan^(-1) * (dx/dy)(360/2pi), where dx and dy are the distances between the COM and snout in the X and Y directions. Angle data were smoothed and differentiated to give a turning rate in degrees per second. Peak, minimum, and average COM and angular velocities and accelerations, turn angle (difference in orientation from start to finish), duration (total time to complete the C-start), and COM distance traveled in 100ms were quantified. Then, the mean for four trials for every individual at each temperature was calculated.

column76: Adult fish were captured by line and hook and were transported to the lab. The fish were induced to spawn with hormone injections, and eggs and sperm were obtained by hand stripping. Eggs were fertilized. To assess hatch rate, time to first hatch, and time to 50% hatch: there were 5 tanks each at their respective test temperature of either 20, 24, 26, 28, or 30°C. Three experimental units, each filled with pre-cleavage-stage eggs, were placed in each bath (pseudoreplication). To assess effect of different temperatures on growth & survival of larvae until 5 days after fertilization: a tank and six hanging PVC units were used for each test temperature of either 20, 24, 26, or 28°C. Every PVC unit had 35 newly-hatched larvae, totaling 210 for each treatment (pseudoreplication b/c each unit is in the same incubator). These larvae were incubated from egg stage. On day 5 after fertilization, live larvae were counted and growth rate was calculated.

column5: Turbot broodstock used in the study were offspring of wild-caught fish from the Black Sea -- I used this location as collection_site & coordinates.
column10: Fish were held at one of four temperatures (10, 14, 18, 22°C) under natural photoperiod and fed with commercial turbot feed to apparent satiation three times a day. Uneaten feed pellets were collected after feeding. Fish were individually weight and measured once a month. Salinity, pH, and dissolved oxygen concentrations were measured weekly. The average pH was estimated as 7.9 +/- 0.1. DO was maintained above 80% throughout the experiment with continuous aeration.
column76: To generate the experimental groups, eggs from a single female were fertilized with milt from two males. Half of the batch was treated with cold shock to induce triploidy. Diplod and triploid fish were reared separately at four constant water temperatures (10, 14, 18, and 22°C). The growth experiment was carried out with 180-day-old hatchery reared turbot.

column5: Upper error values were obtained using webplotdigitizer. Also, weights/lengths weren't given for each experimental group, so I reported them as n/a. However, the fish (total, n = 60 I think) had an average weight of 49.54 +/- 6.72 g and an initial length of 11.70 +/- 0.39 cm. No info on acclimation time, just that the study itself took 60 days.
column10: Pearl cichlids were captured from the sandbanks of Patos Lagoon in Brazil (the fishes had an average weight of 49.54 +/- 6.72 g and an initial length of 11.70 +/- 0.39 cm). In this environment, a salinity of 6, water temperature of 14°C and DO of 10.1 mg/L were recorded. Using a shipping box equipped with oxygen cylinder, the fish were transported to the lab and stored in 200L polyethylene tanks. At the lab, the fish were maintained at a starting temperature of 20°C under constant aeration in 250 L circular tanks. Water was diluted from a salinity of 6 to 0. The tanks were cleaned daily, and renewal of water was performed twice a week. The fish were fed with Guabi pelleted rations containing 40% crude protein, at a rate of 5% of the fishes' biomass. The room temperature was maintained at 17°C.
column49: 60 total fish. 4 fish per tank and 3 replicates per temperature
column76: Sixty G. brasiliensis (n = 4 per experimental unit) were randomly allocated to the experimental treatments from an initial temperature of 20°C. **Each treatment was done in 3 replicates (so sample size for each temperature = 3 x 4 = 12). The fish were starved for 24 hours before receiving snails as prey (these snails {P. canaliculata} were collected from localities with rice paddies). Individual heaters coupled to thermostats increased the water temperature in each experimental unit gradually (1°C/h). Soon after the temperature stabilized, juvenile snails were selected based on their size and distributed (32 per tank). After 18 h of exposure of the snails to predation by the pearl cichlids, all the water in the tanks were passed through a sieve to count the remaining snails. The # of consumed snails and the rate of predation were calculated.
column92: (# of snails predated x 100)/ # of snails offered

column5: This study also had a fluctuating temperature treatment, but I didn't include it. collection_site & coordinates reflect location from which eggs were stripped from wild specimens. These eggs were fertilized in lab. **Sample sizes are not clear -- only tagged fish were used in the growth (total n = 191 tagged fish) but ranges are provided for each temp. So for now, I entered 191/4 = 47.75 to get an average.
column10: Spotted wolffish eggs were fertilized in the autumn of 2002. These eggs were stripped from wild specimens caught off the eastern coast of Iceland (collection_site). The fish were reared in shallow raceways, with their diet adapted to their growth. Water flow was set to 10-15 L/min for each of the experimental units, providing a current speed of 0.5-0.7 cm/s in the raceways. Oxygen was never < 80%. Feed was added daily to the automatic belt feeders. The fish were fed a commercial formulated floating feed, containing 53% protein, 17% fat, and 8% carbohydrate. Feed was provided in excess from automatic feeders from 0900 to 1500 hours. All groups were maintained a constant photoperiod of 18L:6D. In April, the fish were treated for external ectoparasites Ichtyobodo necator and Trichodina sp. with formaldehyde (500 ppm in 30 min).
column76: In preparation for the study, on Nov. 6, 2003, a sub-group within each raceway (n=18-21 in each raceway, ntotal = 191) were tagged intraperitoneally with Trovan Passive Transponder tags and kept at 6°C until the start of the study. The day that growth study began (Dec. 2, 2003), the fish were gradually acclimated over 1 day (4 and 8°C groups) or 3 days (12°C and T-step groups) to the five* (one is fluctuating temperature, which I excluded from the extraction) experimental temperature regumes of 4, 6 (stockfish temperature, 8,12, and temperature-step group. Each temperature regime consisted of two replicate raceways. The 4°C group was reared under an ambient seawater regime. The temperature in all raceways was measured twice daily and remained within +/- 0.2 (SD) of that prescribed. The tagged fish were reared together with 393 untagged fish (30 - 45 in each raceway). All fish were anaesthetized, weighed individually, and total length recorded every 6 weeks. Growth results are based on measurements of tagged fish and other results are based on tank biomass measurements. Feed was provided in excess for 6h daily (0900-1500 hours). Uneaten pellets were collected sfter each feeding and counted to estimate feed intake. The study lasted until June 24, 2004.
column92: G = 100 (e^g - 1), where g = (lnM2 - lnM1)/(t2 - t1) and M2 and M1 are wet masses (g) at days t2 and t1.

column10: A photoperiod of 12L:12D was maintained. Aquaria were stocked with ten-year-old hatchery-reared char, individually marked with fun clips. The fish were fed to satiation with minced beef liver set in gelatine.
column76: The fish were introduced into the aquaria at the same temperature as that of the water in which they were living. Temperatures were then adjusted 1°C/day to their working temperatures. Two aquaria (i.e., two replicates) were adjusted to each of the following temperatures: 4, 8, 12, and 16°C. The fish were allowed to acclimatize to these conditions for 4 weeks, at the end of which time they were anaesthetized, weighed, and measured. After a further period of 4 weeks in their respective temperatures, the fish were again weighed and measured. The temperatures of the 12 and 16°C aquaria were then adjusted to 14 and 18°C, respectively. These four populations of fish were allowed 4 weeks to acclimatize to their new temperatures. They were weighed and measured, left for another 4 weeks, and weighed and measured once more. Specific growth rate, in both terms of length and weight, was calculated for fish at each temperature.

column10: First feeding fry from Magog and Merrimack River genetic strains were brough from their respective hatcheries to the lab. All fish were held in net pens within 175L circular tanks at 10-12°C until the start of the experiment. Fish were fed extruded salmon starter crumbles using automatic feeders. Fish were fed 20 times per day (4 feedings every 5 minutes every 3 hours during the 15 hours of daylight). Photoperiod was 15L:9D for the duration of the experiment to mimic similar daylight in the field.
column76: First feeding fry from Magog and Merrimack River genetic strains were brought from their respective hatcheries to the lab in May, 2001. Specific growth rate was calculated for each strain at six temperatures: 12, 15, 18, 20, 23, and 25°C throughout the 70-day experiment (The experimental period was 70 days, except that Merrimack River 23 and 25°C were terminated after 59 days due to mortality associated with a disconnected air line). Temperature treatments were confined to one tank per temperature and strain. A maximum of ten individuals were placed in each aquarium and allowed to acclimate for one week prior to the start of the experiment. Individuals of each strain were weighed, measured, and uniquely fin clipped. Fish were acclimated to each test temperature for approximately 0.5 h for each 1°C change from 12°C until the test temperature was reached. Fish from each aquarium were weighed every other week throughout the duration of the experiment. Individual growth rates were calculated based on the unique fin clips given each fish. Food was withheld from all aquaria for at least 24 h prior to each weighing even to ensure stomachs were empty.

column5: This paper comprises of 3 experiments: A, B, and C, but only C dealt with wild fish. I extracted the data on the hatchery-reared fish but moved it to the "Notes tab".
column10: The experiments were carried out indoors. The seawater supply was obtained from a well where water was 7°C and salinity 32 per mille. In the growth trials, water exchange was regulated so that the O2 concentration was always above 6 mg/L. Temperatures were adjusted by approximately 1°C/day until target temperatures were reached. This study did three experiments: two on hatchery-reared fish, one on wild fish. Only the latter is present here. The fish had been collected in Faxaflói (a large bay in southwest Iceland) in autumn of 1990. These fish were reared at 7°C for several months prior to the experiment. This experiment lasted 189 days (March 5, 1991 -- September 10, 1991). They were fed once a day on either chopped herring or on whole capelin. The halibut were tagged with numbered spaghetti tags to allow growth rate of individual fish to be calculated. These fish were weighed every 3 months and were not fed 3 days prior to weighing.
column49: each data point is a mean of the performance of 33 fish per temperature treatment. however, some fish died throughout (see final_sample_size) but the authors don't state whether these fish were included in measurements.
column76: Fish were collected in fall 1990 and reared at 7°C for several months prior to the experiment. The fish were divided into six groups with 33 immature fish per group. The rearing experiment lasted for 189 days. Temps of each group were: 2.4, 4.6, 7.0, 9.8, 12.6, and 15.1°C. A natural photoperiod was maintained. The halibut were tagged with numbered spaghetti tags to allow growth rate of individual fish to be calculated. The fish were weighed every 3 months and were not fed for 3 days prior to weighing, and specific growth rates & growth efficiencies were calculated.

column5: two types of swimming: labriform mode at low speeds and switch to undulatory swimming as swimming speed increases. Also, max speeds  were given in both cm/s and BL/s for the same data points. I extracted both . Also, for each performance curve in this paper - there are two points for 30 degrees (1 at normal oxygen levels, one at increased oxygen level).
column10: The fish were kept at 22°C under a 12h:12h light:dark cycle and fed chopped earthworms twice a week.
column49: The 6 fish were tested at each temperature for each metric.
column76: Swimming experiments were carried out at 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30°C in a sealable, recirculating flume. Ambient temperature in the room housing the flume was 22°C. Swimming experiments were carried out at all temperatures in air saturated water, and additionally at 30°C with the dissolved oxygen content elevated to 12.0 mg/L by bubbling 100% oxygen into the water via an air stone. The large volume of water in the flume meant that rapid temperature changes could not be applied using the heaters or chiller. Rates of temperature change were limited to approximately 1°C per hour. Consequently fish could not be exposed to an instantaneous temperature change while in the flume. Exposure to slow temperature changes was undesirable, as this had the potential to allow for at least partial acclimation to temperatures other than Ta. Video sequences were recorded using a Sony HDR HC-3 camcorder at a frame rate of 120 Hz at speeds ranging from 8.4 to a maximum of 51.1·cm·s–1 (0.44–2.68·l·s–1), the upper limit varying with water temperature. Under each set of conditions speed was increased from 8.4·cm·s–1 (0.44·l·s–1) in approximately 4·cm·s–1 (0.21·l·s–1) increments. At each speed the fish was allowed to swim for 5·min before video recording was started. The same group of fish was used for measurements of maximal swimming performance. A protocol involving incremental changes in swimming speed was used to establish Umax using the same group of fish for which kinematic data were obtained. Starting at 8.4·cm·s–1, speed was increased in 4·cm·s–1 increments and maintained at a given level for 10·min between increments. Speed increases continued until the fish could no longer maintain position in the flume. Umax (in cm·s–1)=Ufin+4(T/Tint), where Ufin (in cm·s–1) was the speed of the final interval at which steady swimming could be maintained and TInt was the time interval between speed increments. This test was not equivalent to a critical swimming speed (Ucrit) test. The aim was to determine maximal aerobically supported performance in a similar manner to Claireaux et al. (Claireaux et al., 2006).

The large volume of water in the flume meant that rapid temperature changes could not be applied using the heaters or chiller. Rates of temperature change were limited to approximately 1°C per hour. Consequently fish could not be exposed to an instantaneous temperature change while in the flume. Exposure to slow temperature changes was undesirable, as this had the potential to allow for at least partial acclimation to temperatures other than Ta. Video sequences were recorded using a Sony HDR HC-3 camcorder at a frame rate of 120 Hz at speeds ranging from 8.4 to a maximum of 51.1·cm·s–1 (0.44–2.68·l·s–1), the upper limit varying with water temperature. Under each set of conditions speed was increased from 8.4·cm·s–1 (0.44·l·s–1) in approximately 4·cm·s–1 (0.21·l·s–1) increments. At each speed the fish was allowed to swim for 5·min before video recording was started. The same group of fish was used for measurements of maximal swimming performance. A protocol involving incremental changes in swimming speed was used to establish Umax using the same group of fish for which kinematic data were obtained. Starting at 8.4·cm·s–1, speed was increased in 4·cm·s–1 increments and maintained at a given level for 10·min between increments. Speed increases continued until the fish could no longer maintain position in the flume. Umax (in cm·s–1)=Ufin+4(T/Tint), where Ufin (in cm·s–1) was the speed of the final interval at which steady swimming could be maintained and TInt was the time interval between speed increments. This test was not equivalent to a critical swimming speed (Ucrit) test. The aim was to determine maximal aerobically supported performance in a similar manner to Claireaux et al. (Claireaux et al., 2006).

Swimming experiments were carried out at all temperatures in air saturated water, and additionally at 30°C with the dissolved oxygen content elevated to 12.0 mg/L by bubbling 100% oxygen into the water via an air stone. The large volume of water in the flume meant that rapid temperature changes could not be applied using the heaters or chiller. Rates of temperature change were limited to approximately 1°C per hour. Consequently fish could not be exposed to an instantaneous temperature change while in the flume. Exposure to slow temperature changes was undesirable, as this had the potential to allow for at least partial acclimation to temperatures other than Ta. Video sequences were recorded using a Sony HDR HC-3 camcorder at a frame rate of 120 Hz at speeds ranging from 8.4 to a maximum of 51.1·cm·s–1 (0.44–2.68·l·s–1), the upper limit varying with water temperature. Under each set of conditions speed was increased from 8.4·cm·s–1 (0.44·l·s–1) in approximately 4·cm·s–1 (0.21·l·s–1) increments. At each speed the fish was allowed to swim for 5·min before video recording was started. The same group of fish was used for measurements of maximal swimming performance. A protocol involving incremental changes in swimming speed was used to establish Umax using the same group of fish for which kinematic data were obtained. Starting at 8.4·cm·s–1, speed was increased in 4·cm·s–1 increments and maintained at a given level for 10·min between increments. Speed increases continued until the fish could no longer maintain position in the flume. Umax (in cm·s–1)=Ufin+4(T/Tint), where Ufin (in cm·s–1) was the speed of the final interval at which steady swimming could be maintained and TInt was the time interval between speed increments. This test was not equivalent to a critical swimming speed (Ucrit) test. The aim was to determine maximal aerobically supported performance in a similar manner to Claireaux et al. (Claireaux et al., 2006).

column76: About 300 mackerels (18.29 +/- cm FL) were obtained. They were seasonally separated in four groups and acclimated at different water temperatures (10, 15, 18, and 22°C) for over a week. The fish group of 10°C was obtained in winter (Dec. to Feb.); the group of 15 was collected in sprin (March to May); the group of 18 in autumn (Sept. to Nov.); the group of 22°C was collected in summer (June to Aug.). The tail beat frequency increase following the swimming speed level was observed in the swimming channel of a flume tank (West Japan Fluid Engineering Laboratory, PT-70). The water temperature in the flume tank was maintained at the desired temperature in each fish group (10, 15, 18 and 22 ºC). Each individual was randomly selected and placed in the swimming channel and adapted for 10 minutes to low flow speed (12.4 cm/s) conditions. The tail beat frequency was recorded using a video camera during swimming exercise at various levels of swimming speed, i.e. 20.4, 39.3, 55.4, 74.3, 93.1, 112.0, 128.1, 147.0 and 160.4 cm s-1, being equal to 1.1, 2.1, 3.0, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 7.0, 8.0 and 8.8 FL s-1, respectively. The tail beat frequency of the individual fish at each swimming speed was counted at the slow-motion mode of the video timer. Muscle contraction times were measured using a pair of needles punctured at dorsal muscle of fish body. Minimum muscle contraction time (Tm) data at given temperatures yield maximum tail frequency (Fmax), through an equation as Fmax = 1/2 Tm (Wardle 1975). The maximum swimming speed (Umax) was estimated by a linear regression between tail beat frequency (F) and maximum swimming speed (U, FL s-1) at each temperature, Umax = a + b F.

column10: Fish were housed in filtered municipal water on a recirculating aquaculture system in the Aquatic Life Research Facility in three circular tanks. Upon introduction, fish were held at 12Cin 0.8% marine-grade salt treatment for 5 days to reduce the potential for pathogen outbreak. After being transported to the laboratory, smallmouth bass were surgically implanted with acoustic transmitters. Fish were anaesthetized using tricaine methanesulfonate (TMS), at 120-mg L1 sedation and 60-mg L1 maintenance doses during surgery. Fish remained in holding tanks to recover for >5 days prior to trials and were acclimated to new experimental temperatures by changing their holding tanks by <2C per day. Experiments with the first group of fish were performed at 6, 12, and 18C in sequential order, with temperature acclimation periods of >5 days prior. The second group of fish completed only 24C trials. In each group of fish, two individuals were untagged due to tag number limitations, generating swimming data without acceleration. During holding, each fish was offered one to two crayfish on days occurring >2 days pre- or post-introduction, surgery, or experimentation.

column76: Fish remained in holding tanks to recover for >5 days prior to trials and were acclimated to new experimental temperatures by changing their holding tanks by <2C per day. Experiments with the first group of fish were performed at 6, 12, and 18C in sequential order, with temperature acclimation periods of >5 days prior. The second group of fish completed only 24C trials. In each group of fish, two individuals were untagged due to tag number limitations, generating swimming data without acceleration. Smallmouth bass were transferred individually into a 185-L swim tunnel respirometer. Accelerometer transmitter outputs were measured using a VR100 manual receiver (InnovaSea). Fish were introduced to the swimming portion, the chamber was sealed, and fish were given 5 min to rest. A practice swim was then initiated, beginning with a water flow speed of 10 cm s1, increasing over 3 min to 50 cm s1, and maintaining for 12 min with the chamber sealed. The speed was then reduced to 10 cm s1, and the chamber was flushed with fresh water for 45 min to allow oxygen to replenish and fish to recover. The experimental swimming protocol was then initiated using a ramp-Ucrit design where fish were exposed to swimming speeds starting at 40 cm s1, in 10-cm s1 increments, with 20 min at each speed. When fish did not swim to maintain position in the tunnel, the back grid was electrified to encourage swimming. Three successive shocks with <5 s of resumed swimming in between was the endpoint for each trial, and the time to end was recorded to calculate critical swimming speed. At the end of each experimental day, background respiration was measured in the tunnel by sealing the system for 1 h at 10 cm/s.

column76: The body length of each test fish was measured and placed into the swim chamber to adapt to experimental conditions at 0.5 BL/s for 2 h before the test began (Jain et al. 1997). The temperature and the DO were measured at 10-min intervals until the fish was fatigued (the fish ceases swimming and rests against the grid for 20 s (Lee et al. 2003a). Following fatigue, the flow velocity was decreased to 0.5 BL/s, and the DO was measured at 10-min intervals for 1 h. The fish was then removed from the chamber, and the body mass was recorded. The test data was used to calculate critical swimming speed (Ucirt) and oxygen consumption rate (MO2), and video recordings were analyzed to obtain tail beat frequency (TBF) and TBA.

column10: Fry from all populations were reared under common conditions. Input flows for each tank were set to 600 mL·s−1 and rearing temperatures to 13 ◦C. Emergent trout fry were fed five times per day with BioVita mash (BioOregon, Longview, Washington) and were supplemented with daily infusions of brine shrimp Artemia spp. nauplii. At three weeks post swim-up, the diet was switched over to BioVita starter feed exclusively, which was distributed five times per by day by automatic feeders. Feed rates were adjusted per manufacturers specifications. Tanks were cleaned twice daily to remove uneaten food and waste. Lids were placed over the tanks to simulate overhead cover and reduce disturbance to the fish (Bear et al. 2007), and photoperiod was matched to ambient conditions over the course of the study.

column76: Fertilized trout eggs were collected from four cutthroat trout populations native to Colorado during peak spawning activity in June of 2018. Adult males and females were collected from each population. Families were produced from each of the populations. Each female was stripped into a dry bowl then fertilized with milt from a single male. Fry from all populations were reared under common conditions. Growth trials were conducted by testing each population with three replicates at 6 different temperature treatments. For each population, 18 lots of 15 fish, each representing an even mix of each of the remaining families, were isolated at 126-day post hatch. Target temperatures for each system were 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, and 26 ◦C, maintained with either 800 or 1500 W submersible titanium aquarium heaters with automatic temperature controllers. With different populations reaching the 126-day post-hatch start threshold at different times, it was impossible to acclimate fish by increasing 1 ◦C each day until target temperatures were reached, as in other studies. Accordingly, we acclimated fish by moving their tanks through the temperature ladder provided by the grow-out system baths. For example, fish that were destined to spend 21 days at 23 ◦C were moved from the 13 ◦C round rearing tanks to three 14 ◦C chambers three days prior to the experiment, then to the 17 ◦Cbathtwo days prior, followed by the 20 ◦C bath the day before, reaching the target temperature of 23 ◦C on Day 0. With each transition, the volume of water in the tank was replaced with new (3 ◦C warmer) water over an 18 min period, which served as the tempering phase each day.

Each female was stripped into a dry bowl then fertilized with milt from a single male. Fry from all populations were reared under common conditions. Growth trials were conducted by testing each population with three replicates at 6 different temperature treatments. For each population, 18 lots of 15 fish, each representing an even mix of each of the remaining families, were isolated at 126-day post hatch. Target temperatures for each system were 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, and 26 ◦C, maintained with either 800 or 1500 W submersible titanium aquarium heaters with automatic temperature controllers. With different populations reaching the 126-day post-hatch start threshold at different times, it was impossible to acclimate fish by increasing 1 ◦C each day until target temperatures were reached, as in other studies. Accordingly, we acclimated fish by moving their tanks through the temperature ladder provided by the grow-out system baths. For example, fish that were destined to spend 21 days at 23 ◦C were moved from the 13 ◦C round rearing tanks to three 14 ◦C chambers three days prior to the experiment, then to the 17 ◦Cbathtwo days prior, followed by the 20 ◦C bath the day before, reaching the target temperature of 23 ◦C on Day 0. With each transition, the volume of water in the tank was replaced with new (3 ◦C warmer) water over an 18 min period, which served as the tempering phase each day.

column10: Live juvenile fish of similar size were collected by either fyke net (Arctic and saffron cod), beach seine (Pacific cod), or lift net (walleye pollock) and shipped from a variety of locations to Newport, OR in 2012 (see Table 1 for details). Before use in laboratory experiments, fish were maintained in 1-m-diameter round tanks with flow-through seawater maintained at 6–8 °C.Fish were fed daily by hand to apparent satiation using the gelatinized diet. Apparent satiation was determined as the point where excess food remained in the tank 1 h after feeding. Daily feedings were conducted in this manner across the entire acclimation and experimental period. Lights were maintained on a 12:12 light/dark photoperiod for all experiments. Tanks were checked daily for mortalities, and dead fish were removed, weighed and measured.

column76: For each species, fish were initially measured and stocked into experimental tanks at a density of three individuals/tank. The size range of fish used in the experiments was purposely restricted to focus on the effects of temperature rather than size-dependent growth. After establishment of experimental groups, temperatures were adjusted to treatment temperatures (0, 5, 9, and 16 °C) at a rate of 1.5 °C per day. Replicate tanks (n = 2) of each temperature treatment (n = 4) were assigned for each species (n = 4) to comprise a total of 32 tanks. At week 2 following the acclimation period, fish were weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (wet mass) and measured to the nearest 1 mm (SL) to establish ‘time 0’ for the growth experiment. After measurement, all fish were returned to their original tank and remeasured in the same manner at week 4 (period week 2–week 4) and again at week 6 (period week 4week 6) of the experiment to assess growth. At the end of the experiment, an additional 20 °C trial was conducted for species able to survive and maintain growth at 16 °C during the initial experiment. Fish used for the 20 °C trial were sourced from general holding tanks and had not been used in the original growth experiment. Specific growth rates based on mass of juvenile fish were determined. SGR = 100 - (e^g - 1), where g = ln(WW2) - ln(WW1)/ (t2 - t1). The same approach was used to calculate mean tank growth based on total tank biomass. Notable deviations in the two growth metrics can be an indicator of growth suppression due to social interactions within the tank.

column76: Burbot were caught by trap-nets in Lake P ̈ aij ̈ anne (central Finland) during February–March spawning season. The feeding experiment was performed at four temperatures 2.4, 5.1, 10.8, and 23.4C(S:D:0:49C). Fish were exposed to the natural seasonal water temperature variation between experiments to maximise their acclimation to higher water temperatures during spring and summer. The mean weight of burbot used in the experiment was 296 g .S:D: 48 g; range D 104–353 g; n D 66/ and the mean length 324 mm .S:D:  22 mm; range D 280–380 mm; n D 66/. Burbot .n D 24 initially at each temperature) were randomly selected for the experiment and placed in circular cages .r D 250 mm, h D 750 mm) and then allowed to recover from the handling stress and acclimate to the test environment for 8–14 d (one fish per cage). They were fed vendace at 1–3 d intervals during the acclimation period. During the experiments, the burbot were fed freshly thawed vendace weighing 2.5–3.5 g. For each experiment the average weight of 260 vendace was calculated .mean D 3:02 g, s:d: D 0:11 g) and they were then frozen and stored at −25C. Burbot were fed once a day with 10 whole vendace. After 10 min any vendace remaining in the cage was removed. The number of vendace consumed was recorded and the weight of the meal estimated by multiplying the number of vendace eaten by average weight of vendace in the batch. Burbot that were ill or did not eat were removed from the experiment and the results are based only on data from the healthy animals. Burbot were not reused in the experiment. The total duration of experiments was 21 d at 2.4C, 16 d at 5.1C and 14 d at 10.8C and 23.4C. Mean daily food intake (MDI) values were calculated for each fish (g d−1). Food amounts were also related to burbot weight (RDI, g g−1 d−1) to analyse the effect of burbot size on food intake at different temperatures.

column76: One month before the start of the experiments, mature females were placed in a 400 l aquarium and maintained under standard conditions (food: ad libitum and temp 30°C). Ovary weight was calculated as the difference between the two weights (this method is preferable for determining the weight of small ovaries). column5: the two different collection sites differ in mean water temperature by ca. 3 °C year round with the low-latitude region averaging 23.9 °C in winter and 29.3 °C in summer, compared to 20.8 °C and 27.0 °C in the high-latitude region.
column10: Different coloured tags were used for the two populations to allow fish from the high- and low-latitude populations to be readily distinguished. Fish from each population were then randomly distributed across eight 2000 L round tanks (120 9 150 cm, height 9 diameter) and held under a 13–11 h light–dark regime (subjected to sunrise and sunset as beginning and end of daylight). Tanks were continuously supplied with filtered seawater (salinity 34 ppt) at an initial temperature of 24°C. This temperature corresponded to the temperature ( 2 °C) recorded during field collections. After 4–5 days, the fish assigned to warmer temperatures were slowly brought to their experimental temperature of 27, 30, or 33 °C ( 0.2 °C), with increases in temperature at a maximum rate of 0.5 °C/day. All fish were held at experimental temperatures in fully oxygenated water (equivalent to 44.75, 42.61, 40.67, and 38.92 lg O2/L/mmHg respectively) for a minimum of 4 weeks before experiments began to ensure full metabolic acclimation.
column76: The spontaneous swimming speeds of randomly chosen fish were analysed using Logger Pro v.3.8.6 (Vernier software, Beaverton, OR, USA). In short, based on the dorsal view of the test subject, the x and y coordinates of the tip of the snout and the tip of the caudal fin was manually marked on the first frame. The geometric centre of one of the eyes was then marked on every 10th frame over no less than 150 frames. This provided a record of the change in the x and y coordinates over a period of no less than 5 s. The average rate of spontane ous swimming speeds (i.e. the cumulative distance swum in body length per second, bls1) was then calculated from the positional (x and y) data relative to the total length of the fish. Whenever possible, the source population of the fish (high or low latitude) was recorded based on the colour of the attached T-bar tags. Individuals that could not be identified to population level were recorded as unknown.

column10:
Because the water is stream fed, fish were raised in waters with daily and seasonal variations in temperature (for the 2-year period when fish were
raised, daily mean was 9.10 C and standard deviation was 0.98 C). Except for eyed eggs for Slate Island, all eggs were brought to Codrington as fertilized eggs. The eggs were reared in family partitioned Heath trays until hatching and were then moved to 60 L family specific tanks that were divided in two to hold two separate families (McDermid et al., 2013). The size and amount of optimum salmonid feed (Corey Nutrition Co., redericton, NB, Canada) was evaluated on a monthly basis to allow for maximum growth using the recommended feeding
guide for salmonids provided by the feed supplier. The size of the feed was adjusted to match the mean size of the fish and the amount of feed was dependent on the biomass in the tanks (mean biomass specific to the strains). The biomass was monitored closely to avoid exceeding 34 g/L to ensure maximum growth. Fish were clipped to identify families (January 2016) and pit-tagged (October 2016) to track individuals.

column76: RMR trials began in the morning at approximately the same time throughout the experiment. Although we stopped feeding the fish 40 h prior to the experiment, our metabolic measurements were taken on growing juvenile lake trout (not on a maintenance ration) and are therefore growth-inflated metabolic rates. Flow rates were low enough so that fish were inactive (not swimming), and the chambers were narrow enough so that fish could not turn around. fish were transferred to the chambers the afternoon prior to RMR measurements allowing them 16 hrs to acclimate to their new surroundings. Fish had at least 40 hrs following their last feeding before experiments were conducted in order to remove the effect of digestion on RMR readings (Allen et al., 2016). Oxygen consumption rates were recorded for three, 5 min intervals with a 5 min flush period between each measurement to allow fresh water to enter the system and replenish the oxygen.  MMR tests were performed on two fish simultaneously (one per rtechnician) and involved measuring oxygen consumption on fish that were exhausted by implementing a chase protocol (Clark et al., 2013).Once fish were exhausted (3 to 8 min), they were quickly transferred to the respirometry chamber and the flush pump was turned off and on for eight consecutive 5 min oxygen consumption measurements over a 75 min period.  Aerobic performance was assessed by comparing the time to exhaustion and metabolic recovery of each strain (Clark et al., 2013).

column76: The absorption efficiency was determined using the Conover (1966) method. For this, we determined the organic fraction of representative samples of the faeces from H. antarcticus and the diet supplied (i.e., G. antarctica). Samples of food and faeces were filtered through pre-ashed, pre-weighed, 25-mm glass fiber filters, rinsed with isotonic ammonium formate, dried to a constant weight at 80 °C, weighed, combusted at 450 °C for 3 h, and weighed again to estimate the organic and inorganic fraction contained in the food and faeces. The absorption rate was calculated as the product of the organic ingestion rate and absorption efficiency. For each fish, ingestion and absorption rates were averaged over time (n = 5) before conducting the statistical analyses

column10: In the laboratory, fish were kept in wooden, glass-fronted, continuous-flow, holding tanks (86.5 X 46 X 30 cm; water height, 25 cm) of 99.5 L capacity. All tanks were equipped with inflows, outflows, heaters, and regulators. Tests were run at six test temperatures: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. Each series was duplicated. Biomasses of fish in the tanks were equivalent at the start of the experiments: 31-42 g wet weight for year 0 and 102- 140 g for the year 2 fish. The numbers of fish per tank were 8- 10 for the smaller and 3-5 for the larger size group. Within each tank, sizes of indi- viduals were varied slightly so that the growth history of each indi- vidual could be followed; this and observing feeding were used as a means of monitoring health. (Bullheads do not exhibit the dominance hierarchy that may lead to differential growth rates in centrarchids (A. Keast, unpublished data).) Positions of the tanks were random ized. Day length was on a 12 h light : 12 h dark schedule. Kingston municipal water, dechlorinated by passage through charcoal filters, was used (67 mg CaC03/L, pH 7.2).

All tanks were equipped with inflows, outflows, heaters, and regulators. Tests were run at six test temperatures: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. Each series was duplicated. Biomasses of fish in the tanks were equivalent at the start of the experiments: 31-42 g wet weight for year 0 and 102- 140 g for the year 2 fish. The numbers of fish per tank were 8- 10 for the smaller and 3-5 for the larger size group. Within each tank, sizes of indi- viduals were varied slightly so that the growth history of each indi- vidual could be followed; this and observing feeding were used as a means of monitoring health. (Bullheads do not exhibit the dominance hierarchy that may lead to differential growth rates in centrarchids (A. Keast, unpublished data).) Positions of the tanks were random ized. Day length was on a 12 h light : 12 h dark schedule. Kingston municipal water, dechlorinated by passage through charcoal filters, was used (67 mg CaC03/L, pH 7.2).

column5: This population was introduced in 1999 (Mitchell and Purchase 2014) from Indian Bay, NL (COSEWIC 2014). Embryos were collected on artificial (yarn, 10- to 15-cm-long threads) spawning mops (20), which were used to mimic the plant substrate that banded killifish eggs typically adhere to. The mops were checked twice daily. Embryos stripped from the mops during the first collection were not used because fertilization time (within 20h) was unknown. The second collection took place 4h later, and therefore, embryos were known to be within the first 4 h of development. Individual embryos were fully immersed in water in Petri dishes placed in incubators at their respective temperatures, and the water was topped up daily. Each individual embryo was checked under a dissecting microscope for cell division to ensure fertilization, and embryos from each collection day were distributed evenly into the different treatments (Figure 2). The majority of the embryos were collected between 27 June and 1 July (n 1⁄4 84). Because of low hatch success at the lower temperatures, we collected additional embryos (n 1⁄4 23; between 9 and 11 July) and added them evenly into the 10 and 16 C levels to increase the sample size.

column76: Fish were removed from their acclimation tanks with a dip net and placed in a Loligo mini swim tunnel respirometer (Loligo Systems, Tjele, Denmark) containing 20 ppt water at the acclimation temperature of the fish. The tunnel was set at the lowest speed possible to minimize stratification of water oxygen concentrations but to avoid the fish actively swimming against the current. Fish were allowed 30 min to adjust to the respirometer before the onset of measurement. After the 30-min recovery time, the tunnel was sealed, and the decrease in water oxygen concentration over time, measured using NeoFox oxygen probes (Ocean Optics, Dunedin, FL) with a sampling rate of once every 15 s, was used to calculate mass- specific M ̇ O2routine, as in Sloman et al. (2008) and Fangue et al. (2009b). Fish remained quiescent during the measurement pe- riod, and the oxygen trace interval that gave a constant rate of decrease for at least 5 min and resulted in the lowest M ̇ O2 was used to calculate M ̇ O2routine. The respirometers were rinsed daily with a 75% ethanol solution, which resulted in negligible bacterial respiration (!1% of total oxygen consumption) in all trials. Note that M ̇ O2routine was measured once per fish.

column76: Indi- vidual fish were placed into 27.5×17.5 cm plastic aquaria (hereafter, ‘arenas’) housed in a recirculating water bath after they were measured in mm TL and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (Table 1). To prevent fish from seeing other individuals during the trail, the sides of the arenas were painted black. A recirculating chiller or submersible heater was used to maintain the water temperature in the water bath appropriate for the temperature treatment being tested. Each arena was kept aerated while housing fish. Arenas were placed over a 2 cm × 2 cm grid on a white background. Fish were habit- uated to the arenas for 7 days and fed a ration of frozen bloodworms each day during this period. Fish were fasted for 48 h before we stationed a GoPro® camera above each individual arena, capturing the entire arena in the field of view. The aerator was removed from the arena during video recording to prevent agitation of the water’s surface. Fish were recorded continuously for 15 min (Gautrias et al., 2009; Troia et al., 2016). We discarded the first 5 min of video to account for fish potentially being disturbed when the camera was turned on. Activity was quantified from the subsequent 10 min of video by randomly selecting a subsample of 10 non- overlapping 30-s intervals during the filmed trail and calculat- ing the average number of 2 cm × 2 cm grids the fish traversed per unit time. All 12 fish belonging to a single acclimation temperature were filmed on the same day, beginning at 0900 h and finishing within 2 h. During filming trials, we recorded two fish concurrently using different cameras. Filming for all five acclimation treatments was completed in 5 days.

To prevent fish from seeing other individuals during the trail, the sides of the arenas were painted black. A recirculating chiller or submersible heater was used to maintain the water temperature in the water bath appropriate for the temperature treatment being tested. Each arena was kept aerated while housing fish. Arenas were placed over a 2 cm × 2 cm grid on a white background. Fish were habit- uated to the arenas for 7 days and fed a ration of frozen bloodworms each day during this period. Fish were fasted for 48 h before we stationed a GoPro® camera above each individual arena, capturing the entire arena in the field of view. The aerator was removed from the arena during video recording to prevent agitation of the water’s surface. Fish were recorded continuously for 15 min (Gautrias et al., 2009; Troia et al., 2016). We discarded the first 5 min of video to account for fish potentially being disturbed when the camera was turned on. Activity was quantified from the subsequent 10 min of video by randomly selecting a subsample of 10 non- overlapping 30-s intervals during the filmed trail and calculat- ing the average number of 2 cm × 2 cm grids the fish traversed per unit time. All 12 fish belonging to a single acclimation temperature were filmed on the same day, beginning at 0900 h and finishing within 2 h. During filming trials, we recorded two fish concurrently using different cameras. Filming for all five acclimation treatments was completed in 5 days.
