column76: We used a 5-L swim tunnel respirometer (Loligo Systems, Tjele, Denmark) to carry out swimming performance trials (Svendsen et al., 2015). We included eight dace and eight stonerollers in each of five temperature treatments (10, 15, 20, 25 and 30◦ C; total n = 80). We used either submersible heaters or ice packs to maintain water temperature in the swim tunnel within0.2◦Cofthetemperaturetreatmentbeingtested.Trials of critical swimming velocity (Ucrit) were conducted using a velocity increment based on the total length (TL) of the fish (Brett, 1964; Morozov et al., 2018). Before being introduced to the swim chamber, individual fish were measured in mm TL and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (Table 1). To discourage the fish from attempting to rest against the back screen of the swim chamber, we placed a partitioning shade over the front half of the chamber and shined light at the back of the chamber. Following methods for other fish species, fish were first acclimated to the chamber with no flow velocity for 30 min (Lehman et al., 2017) and then for 10 min at a water velocity of 1 TL s−1 before beginning the experiment. Swimming trials began at a water velocity of 2 TL s−1, with velocity being increased by 1 increment (1 TL) every 5 min and ending once the fish was fatigued (Nelson et al., 2003). Fatigue was determined as the velocity at which the fish became pinned to the back of the swim tunnel and would not return to swimming after visual or acoustic stimuli.

column76: Burst swimming responses were assessed in a 35 × 24 × 4 cm aquarium with a 20 cm measuring tape placed in the field of view for calibration. The aquarium was secured inside an arena made of plywood and a mirror angled at 45°. A Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ40 camera recorded the image at 100 frames per second off the mirror. Burst swimming responses were elicited by gently tapping the fish’s tail using a metal rod when fish were motionless on the bottom of the tank. Instantaneous swimming speed was extracted from videos using KINOVEA© [experimental version 0.8.25-x64 (http://www.kinovea.org)]. Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response were analysed. The point between the eyes of each fish was digitised to ensure a consistent point was tracked. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined. The maximum instantaneous speeds for each fish were averaged at each test temperature and used in statistical analysis.

column76: We quantified the maximum ventilation and metabolic rate of each individual fish at 15 °C, 22 °C, 28 °C, 33 °C, and 36 °C (and 12 °C for ventilation rate only) in a randomised order. We tested maximum ventilation rate by chasing a fish (with a hand net) for a minute to elicit a sustained escape response. Fish were then immediately placed into a transparent petri dish and filmed ventrally for 60 s using a Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ40 camera at a rate of 100 frames per second. Ventilation rate was then determined by visually counting the number of operculum ventilations over 60 s. Immediately after ventilation rate was filmed, fish were placed in a 133 mL respirometer with a magnetic stirrer that produced a current within the respirometer for the fish to swim against (the current was turned up until fish could just maintain forward movement within the water column) to assess maximum metabolic rate. A PreSens Fibox 4 (POF-L2.5-1) with a polymer optical fiber and oxygen minisensor spots (batch ID—140117-001) was used to measure percentage air saturation (% a.s.) (one measurement/second) within the respirometer over 5 min of testing. After individual fish were tested, they were then placed in an oxygen-saturated recovery bucket where the water temperature changed at a rate of 3 °C/h to bring the fish back to their treatment conditions. Three control (no fish) water samples were taken at each test temperature over 5 min to assess for any oxygen consumption or production within the bottle during testing.

column49: Each tank was randomly assigned to either a high (ad libitum) or low (3 % body weight d– 1 on a wet weight basis) ration level. There were 6 replicate tanks for each temperature/ration treatment. Because the 2 fish in a tank were closely similar in size and prior experi- ments have suggested minimal differences in food acquisition even between disparately sized sablefish (Sogard & Olla 2000), we expected them to have equal access to food.
column76: Conversion efficiency was calculated for fish held individually in 82 l tanks (n = 12 replicates per temper- ature) in a flow-through system during 3 wk experi- ments in 1999 (Table 1). Fish were randomly assigned a low (3% body weight [bw] d–1 on a wet weight basis) or high (ad libitum) ration. Temperatures tested were 6, 10, 16, 20, and 22°C. Temperatures were ambient (mean = 12°C) when fish were introduced to tanks, and gradually increased or decreased at a rate of 2°C d–1 to the target level during the first week. Fish received either 2 or 3 mm BioDiet pellets (composition noted above) distributed from automatic feeders over a 1 h period. Pellets remaining in tanks after the feeding period were counted and removed by siphoning. The total number of pellets consumed each week by each fish was determined and the dry weight of food con- sumed calculated from previously determined rela- tionships.

column76: At the conclusion of experiments conducted in 1999, groups were randomly selected for measurement of swimming activity levels. Prior to final length and weight measurements, groups were transferred to circular (122 cm diameter), 340 l tanks filled with water of the same temperature used during growth evaluation. After a 30 min acclimation period, groups were video- taped with overhead cameras. There were 4 replicate groups from each ration/temperature treatment, with the exception of the 24°C treatment, which had only 1 tank with survivors in the high ration treatment. Each group was filmed for 1 h; no food was present during filming. Videotapes were analyzed with an image analysis system using a digitizing pen to trace the movement of individual fish. Each fish of a pair was tracked for 30 s, with 4 sets of observations at approxi- mately 10 min intervals. Due to the shallow water depth (30 cm), movement occurred primarily in the horizontal plane, justifying use of the overhead 2- dimensional video image to assess activity. The average speed of fish (body lengths s–1) moving through the tank was calculated for each interval and averaged overall for each group.

column76: Routine oxygen uptake (RMR) was measured from the decline in dissolved oxygen saturation of water within two custom-made, intermittent-flow, airtight and lightproof respirometers 8.0× 15.5×22.5 cm. Gut evacuation from repletion in B. saida took 36– 70 h at −1.5 to −0.5°C, with an average of 51 h (Hop et al., 1997). Thus, after a 48 h fasting period, a fish was transferred to each of the two respirometers, which were connected to a 32 litre, closed-circuit sump that contained two refrigerant coils attached to two programmable chillers (Fisher Isotemp 3016d; www.fisherssci.com) filled with 60% propylene glycol antifreeze. The seawater sump was continuously aerated and also held a magnetic drive pump. Water temperature was controlled by the recirculating chillers and measured to a precision of ±0.1°C (Fisher Scientific Type K digital thermometer probe). A pilot experiment that measured oxygen uptake over 47.5 h while wild-caught B. saida became accustomed to the respirometer found that RMR stabilized between 12 h and 22 h (see Fig. 2A, inset). Consequently, all RMR measurements began following an overnight acclimation of minimally 12 h. Water temperature was adjusted at a rate of 3°C h−1 to the desired acute test temperature for that experiment: 0.5, 2.0, 3.5, 5.0 and 7.5°C for the 3.5°C acclimation group, and 0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.5 and 8.5°C for the 1.0°C and 6.5°C acclimation groups. At the test temperature, fish were held for 1 h before measuring RMR using closed respirometry that recorded the depletion of oxygen from the water with a fibre optic oxygen meter for up to 30 min (Firesting O2, PyroScience, Aachen, Germany). This procedure was repeated 2-3 times and the lowest value was reported as RMR. Then, the fish was removed from the respirometer and placed in a ∼12 litre circular tank containing aerated water at the test temperature for exhaustive exercise. Chasing involved a 5 min period of hand chasing, gentle tail pinches and lifting until unresponsive to touch, followed by brief air exposure (Norin and Clark, 2016). The fish was returned to the respirometer and oxygen uptake measurement resumed within 30 s and continued over 5–30 min, depending on the test temperature. The maximum oxygen uptake (MMR) was calculated from the steepest 2–5% decrease in percentage water saturation, which occurred consistently at the start of recording. Water oxygen saturation never decreased below 75% saturation for any measurement. After the MMR measurement, fish were weighed, pit tagged (if newly tested) and returned to their acclimation tank. AAS was calculated as MMR −RMR and factorial aerobic scope (FAS) as MMR/RMR. Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) was measured at 0.5 and 1 h after MMR to compare the % return to initial RMR values for the 1.0°C and 6.5°C acclimated fish. Tests with the 1.0°C acclimation group used 20 fish bred at the Vancouver Aquarium with a mean mass of 59.8±2.7 g. Tests with the 3.5°C acclimation group used 19 wild fish caught in 2011 with a mean mass of 111.5±6.1 g. Tests with the 6.5°C acclimation group used 11 fish bred at the Vancouver Aquarium and 6 wild fish caught in 2012 with a mean mass of 74.1±7.6 g.

column49: We measured sustained swimming performance and resting and recovery oxygen con- sumption (MO2) in the same five fish from each replicate tank (n p 5 fish # 3 replicates p 15 fish per acclimation treat- ment).
column76: Swimming performance was measured as the critical sustained swimming speed (Ucrit; Brett 1965) in an oval doughnut-shaped flume (2.32 m long # 1.10 m wide [0.32 m width of the swimming lane] # 0.70 m deep). During swimming trials, fish were individually contained in a restricted space (0.41 m long # 0.32 m wide # 0.70 m deep) within which laminar flow was approximated by a series of baffles. Unidirectional flow was produced by an electric outboard motor (Riptide RT40, Minn Kota, Mankato, MN), which was regulated with a variable DC power supply (MP3090, Powertech, Melbourne). Flow was proportional to the voltage output of the power sup- ply, and the power supply settings were calibrated using a flow probe (FP101, GlobalWater, Gold River, CA; sensitive to 0.01 m s1) so that voltage output could be related to water velocity in the restricted swimming space. The flume was situated in a temperature-controlled room, and water temperature was ad- ditionally regulated by two immersion heaters (Julabo Ther- momix, Seelbach, Germany). Fish were introduced into the flume enclosure for 10 min before experimen- tation to equilibrate body temperature to water temperature (Seebacher 1999). Each fish was swum at 12, 14, 17, 22, and 26C, with at least 24 h between swimming trials. The order of test temperature at which fish were swum was randomly allocated (Hammill et al. 2004). The body length (mouth to caudal fin tip) of each fish was measured after swimming trials, and recovery MO2 measurements and Ucrit were corrected for body length (BL) and presented as BL s1. A fish was considered to be fatigued when it could no longer hold its position in the water column after a gentle prod with a plastic rod.
column92: highest swimming speed (Uf) + (time to fatigue/interval between speed increments) * speed increment (Ui)

column76: Burst-swimming performance was assessed by videotaping at least four swimming sequences for each individual at each temperature. Burst-swimming responses were elicited by placing adults in a swimming arena and tapping their dorsal surface with a ®ne probe, usually resulting in a C-start and several propulsive strokes <one startle response). Only startle responses from a stationary position that produced C-start responses were used in the analysis of burst swimming performance. Burst-swimming sequences were videotaped in a temperature controlled <M0.5°C) 1.00 m  ́ 0.40 m  ́ 0.25 m deep Perspex tank. Swimming responses were videotaped by recording the image at an angle of 90° above the arena using a ±1 video camera recording at 50 frames  was analysed to determine the maximum velocity <Umax distance moved throughout the initial 200 ms <D 200 taken to reach U max <T-Umax). We used a Hitachi video recorder <Model VT-L1000E) to play back the re- corded sequences frame by frame, with the image projected onto a 1.5 m  ́ 1.5 m screen. The approximate centre of mass of each ®sh <one-third the length of the total length) was manually digitised for each frame during a startle response, with the distance be- tween each mark measured. The start of a swimming sequence was deened as the frame immediately preceding the frame where movement was first detected, with the movement of the sh measured each frame for 300 ms. Velocity of the ®sh was deter mined by calculating the distance moved between each frame <i.e. 20 ms). The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual at each temperature was used as a measure of their maximum burst swimming performance.

Eggs were obtained from a ripe (eggs run with slight pressure) female caught in Lake Constance in May 1991 and fertilized by the dry method (cf. Craig, 1987 ) with the milt of two males. The egg strand was cut into subsamples of 76-125 eggs. Each subsample was first placed into a jar which stood in the baths of 10 or 12 oC, and then each jar was repeatedly transferred to the next bath with 2 oC higher or lower temperature at 5- 10 min. intervals until the final tem- perature was reached. Four jars in each bath were used to estimate the hatch rate. The fifth jar in each bath contained about 200 eggs, which were used to observe the embryonic development throughout the incubation period and to determine the total lengths of larvae at mass hatching (50% hatching). Water was renewed twice a day and continuous aeration was supplied by Pasteur pipettes. When over 90% of the embryos had hatched, they were counted and expressed as a percent- age of the egg number counted previously, i.e. hatch rate. The hatched larvae were transfered to a 500 ml jar to observe the swim-up stage.

column76: Burst swimming speed was assessed to gain a whole- organism measure of performance capacity at all test temperatures (see detailed methods in Seebacher et al. 2014). Fish were placed in an 8 cm 9 10 cm testing aquarium with a fixed 10-cm measuring tape placed in the field of view for calibration. A high-speed camera (Pana- sonic Lumix DMC-TZ40) was set up directly above the middle of the testing aquarium and recorded the image. Burst swimming responses were promoted by tapping next to the fish’s tail using a thin metal rod when fish were stationary. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish, and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined and extracted from videos using the program KINOVAÓ (ex- perimental version 0.8.25-x64). Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response (pow- erful escape response where fish bends body into C shape to flick tail for rapid burst movement) were analysed. We digitised the point between the eyes of each fish to ensure consistent tracking. Maximum instantaneous speeds for individual fish were averaged at each acute test temperature.

A high-speed camera (Pana- sonic Lumix DMC-TZ40) was set up directly above the middle of the testing aquarium and recorded the image. Burst swimming responses were promoted by tapping next to the fish’s tail using a thin metal rod when fish were stationary. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish, and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined and extracted from videos using the program KINOVAÓ (ex- perimental version 0.8.25-x64). Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response (pow- erful escape response where fish bends body into C shape to flick tail for rapid burst movement) were analysed. We digitised the point between the eyes of each fish to ensure consistent tracking. Maximum instantaneous speeds for individual fish were averaged at each acute test temperature.

column49: each point represents the percentage of normal developing larvae (NDL) calculated per tank (i.e., per replicate), at a given incubation temperature. For each temperature, they incubated replicate tanks (typically 6 per temperature, except 4 at 9°C). There were about 100 eggs in each tank
column76: Egg veils were collected from coastal waters using a scoop net and transported to the lab. The egg veils were cut into ~2–3 cm squares, each containing about 100 eggs. Egg pieces were placed into small tanks (500 mL) filled with artificial seawater (salinity 32–33). Incubation was performed at six different temperatures: 9°C, 13°C, 15°C, 18°C, 21°C, and 24°C. Water temperature was adjusted gradually before incubation began. twice daily, hatched larvae and dead embryos were counted. Hatched larvae were preserved in ethanol for assessment. Deformities were checked under a stereomicroscope. Deformed larvae showed issues like bent or stunted notochords or jaws. Percentage of NDL (normal developing larvae, i.e., non-deformed live larvae) to the total collected individuals was calculated.

column76: Fish were placed individually in darkened, temperature-controlled respirometry chambers and allowed 90 minutes to acclimate. column10: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. In spring 2021, males and females were placed in separate tanks and gradually induced into spawning by increasing temperature and photoperiod. After 3 weeks on a rich diet, gametes were collected in vitro from 20 females and 10 males per population. Eggs and milt from each population were pooled, mixed, and fertilized in Petri dishes. column76: Oxygen consumption rates were measured for groups of schooling fish (n = 6–25) instead of individuals, because individually separated clupeids are hyperactive, lose scales and die due to stress (Hettler 1976; Blaxter and Hunter 1982). At the end of an experiment, fish were removed and rapidly killed by an overdose of anaesthetic (MS-222) and weighed individually (0.001 g accuracy). After fish were transferred into the respirometer chamber, they firstly showed very high oxygen consumption due to handling stress, i.e. acclimation phase. This initial phase was not included in the data analysis. The separation between acclimation and routine phase followed the procedure of Herrmann and Enders (2000). For calculations of metabolic rates, only data of the routine phase were used. Taking into account the chamber volume and the displaced volume of the fish, the actual oxygen uptake rate in one measuring interval in mgO2 h-1 of the fish group was calculated by linear regression of oxygen concentration on time. Only oxygen consumption rates with a regression coefficient [0.9 times the average of all regression coef- ficients (*0.97) were selected to calculate metabolic rates (Herrmann and Enders 2000). The total oxygen uptake was then divided by numbers of fish and fish wet weight after values for bacterial respiration were subtracted. Standard metabolism (RS) was calculated as the median of the lower 10% of the respiration rates in the routine phase over one experiment (Herrmann and Enders 2000). For the calculation of routine metabolism (RR), all oxygen consumption values of the routine phase have been used

column76: Oxygen consumption was quantified as part of a series of seven sequential temperature‐exposure trials conducted between 14 August and 24 September 2005. All fish were initially acclimated to 16 °C for three weeks before experimentation began. Each trial lasted six days and exposed fish to a fixed test temperature that increased by 2 °C increments across trials (18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 °C), except the final trial, which used 27 °C due to mortality at 28 °C. At the start of each trial, fish from two age classes (0+ and 2+) were randomly assigned to individual respirometers. For each age class, treatment fish were held in a tank system in which water temperature was increased to the target test temperature, while control fish remained at 16 °C.  All respirometers initially operated as open, flow-through systems. Once fish were placed inside, test-system water was gradually warmed by 2 °C over 2 h to reach the trial’s experimental temperature. Pre-measurement conditions - Behavioural monitoring occurred from days 1–3, after which fish were food-deprived for 42 h to ensure a postabsorptive state (avoiding digestion-related increases in metabolic rate). Oxygen consumption measurements began at 11:00 on day 5. For oxygen measurements, the respirometers were switched from flow-through to closed systems. Oxygen concentrations inside each chamber were recorded for a minimum of 90 minutes for individual fish.
column92:
O2 consumed = [(deltaO2) - BODblanks) * V*(60T^-1)]/W
Where DeltaO2) was the difference between the final oxygen level in the respirometer and the initial level (mg L)1), BOD (mg L)1) was biological (microbial) respiration once the fish was removed, V was the volume of the container (5Æ7 L for 0+ and 11Æ3 L for 2+ Atlantic salmon), T was the duration of the measurement (min) and W was the wet weight of the fish (grams). The volume of the respirometer was not adjusted for the volume of the fish.

column76: Oxygen consumption (Mo₂) was measured using automated intermittent-flow respirometry in temperature-controlled water baths. Each respirometer had two loops: a closed loop with an oxygen sensor that logged dissolved oxygen every 2 seconds, and a flush loop used to replenish oxygen so levels stayed above 80% saturation. Metabolic rate was calculated only during the closed periods, because that’s when the fish’s breathing is the only thing causing oxygen to drop. RMR calculation -- Because the two study sites used different protocols, all minimum metabolic rates were standardized as RMR. Lake Victoria fish underwent a chase protocol and required a longer recovery, so RMR was calculated from the lowest 10% of Mo₂ values collected during a 9-hour post-exercise period, excluding outliers. Lake Nabugabo fish were transferred into chambers without chasing and recovered more quickly, but only two low, stable Mo₂ values were available. Recovery tests (Nyboer & Chapman 2017) showed that Nile perch reached baseline metabolism after ~180 min post-chase and ~140 min post-transfer. To ensure comparability across lakes, only Mo₂ measurements taken after 140 minutes were used for RMR calculations in both datasets. For Lake Nabugabo fish, this corresponded to the two measurements collected after this threshold.

column76: fish respirometry chambers the night before experiments to ensure post-absorptive status. Chambers were submerged in a temperature-controlled, aerated 300-L fiberglass tank set to each fish’s acclimation temperature, with black plastic sheeting used to minimize disturbance. Dissolved oxygen was maintained >95% saturation using air stones and, at warm temperatures, a wet-dry trickle column. Resting metabolic rate (RMR) was measured using intermittent respirometry, with alternating flush and sealed measurement periods. During each sealed period, water samples were taken at the start and end to determine PO₂ using a polarographic electrode; O₂ concentrations (mg O₂ L⁻¹) were calculated using established nomograms. Three measurement periods were completed per fish, and mean O₂ decline was used to calculate RMR. After trials, fish mass and length were recorded. RMR was expressed as a mass-independent rate, scaled using a 0.79 mass exponent.

column76: Fish were anesthetized, weighed, and placed in a well-aerated bath with their gills continuously irrigated. ECG electrodes were placed on the heart to record heart rate. Heart rate was stimulated with injections of atropine and isoproterenol and allowed to stabilize for ~20 minutes. Water temperature was gradually increased or decreased in steps until the fish showed heart rhythm problems or the bath started to freeze. the maximum heart rate and its temperature, and the temperature where the heart became arrhythmic. Heart rate data were analyzed using segmented regression to find points where heart function was affected by temperature.

column76: Fish were captured and allowed to recover overnight (>12 h). They were warmed to the test temperature at 2 °C h⁻¹, held 1 h, then chased to fatigue (≈4.4 min). After chasing, fish experienced ~1.3 min of air exposure, during which a small caudal blood sample (~200 µL) was taken. Fatigue was defined as not responding to touch for >5 s. Fish were immediately sealed into a 30-L intermittent-flow respirometer. MMR was calculated from the steepest decline in dissolved oxygen during any measurement period using an automated algorithm.

column76: In 2012, creek side repeat swimming performance tests were conducted on a subset of juvenile Arctic char (smolts) over the range of naturally occurring temperatures to assess the effect of temperature on cardiorespiratory performance.  90 L swim tunnel respirometer with a 70 × 20 × 20 cm test section (Loligo). A small electrical charge (<6 V) was applied to the rear gate of the test section to motivate fish to swim. Fish were allowed to acclimate at a low water speed (0.5 body lengths/s; bl/s) for 30 min after which the speed was increased by 0.5 bl/s every 10 min until the fish fatigued and was not able to remove itself from the rear gate within 5 s. Fish were then allowed to recover for 30 min at 0.5 bl/s and were then given a second swim test except speed was increased every 1 min rather than every 10 min. The 30-min recovery time was intentionally shorter than previous studies (Jain et al., 1998; MacNutt, Hinch, Farrell, & Topp, 2004) to assess the capacity of the fish to recover rapidly. The short step length in the second test was selected (Farrell, 2008) as a rapid assessment of recovery in order to limit the duration of the static temperature expo- sure and increase throughput under time constraints in the field. The Brett equation (Brett, 1964) was used to calculate the critical swimming speed for each test (test 1: Umax1; test 2: Umax2) and the quotient of (recovery ratio; RR) and difference between these values were considered measures of recovery (Jain et al., 1998).

column76: Maximum daily consumption was measured by feeding northern squawfish ad libitum on juvenile salmonids over a 48-hour period at controlled temperatures. Only healthy, active fish were used. Fish were fasted long enough to empty their stomachs, using temperature-specific gut evacuation equations. Groups were stratified into weight classes. Fish were fed juvenile Chinook and Coho salmon to satiation. Feeding occurred  at the start of the trial then every 4 hours (total of 14 feedings). Final feeding at hour 47.5. Final body weight of each predator was measured with stomach contents removed (±1 g). Maximum daily ration was calculated as: (Total prey consumed in centigrams) / (Total predator mass in grams) / 24 h reported as cg·g⁻¹·day⁻¹
